open_obligations: Check how Kenton et al.'s debaters were trained; the cited passage does not say, so Khan et al.'s deceptive-model concern is not addressed.
Check that Gemini Pro 1.5 debaters are actually stronger reasoners than each of the other judges on each task.
Check that the baseline differs: Kenton et al. compare with direct QA, Khan et al. with naive judges.
in.other_title: Closed QA without information asymmetry: debate vs direct QA depends on judge strength
in.rationale: Khan et al. note their expertise gap is only access to information, whereas future models may differ in reasoning. Kenton et al. test closed tasks without information asymmetry and report debate beats consultancy but versus direct QA is mixed: GPT-3.5 benefits (p = 0.037), Pro 1.0 shows no statistically significant difference (p = 0.1) and Gemma7B and Pro 1.5 do worse. The Pro 1.5 judge is the same model as the debaters, so that case has no weak-strong asymmetry and, the authors say, does not inform much about scalable oversight; they read GPT-3.5 and Pro 1.0 as probably the most indicative of scalable oversight, showing small or no benefit of debate over QA without article. The cited Kenton et al. passage does not address Khan et al.'s concern that debate may not suit deceptive models.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate's benefit holds when debaters and judge differ in capability rather than information access, for closed QA with LLM judges

open_obligations: Check that the toy-setting remark applies to Khan et al. [13] and not only to Radhakrishnan [23], which is grouped with it and is not in the atlas
Do not extend the toy-setting remark to Irving et al. [12], which is cited in the same group but does not use QuALITY
Check that the 'judges have not read' description matches Khan et al.'s hidden-passage protocol
The cited passage stops at 'invaluable for early scalable oversight'; check the next line for what the authors say the toy setting lacks
in.other_title: Prior debate evidence described as a toy setting of short stories judges have not read
in.rationale: McAleese et al. say previous work [12, 13, 23] has demonstrated that oversight methods like debate have the potential to help humans more accurately assess the answers to reading comprehension questions, and their reference list gives [13] as Khan et al., Debating with more persuasive LLMs leads to more truthful answers (2402.06782). They note these works apply their methods primarily to multiple choice questions about short science fiction stories that the judges have not read, and say that toy setting was invaluable for early scalable oversight. Khan et al. state as a limitation that in their setup the difference between strong and weak is only in access to information. The remark bears on that limitation, since it calls the setting of works including Khan et al., where the judges have not read the stories, a toy setting. The cited lines stop before saying what the toy setting lacks and do not argue that the difference is only in access to information, so the remark is not an argument for Khan et al.'s limitation and the link proposes only ADDRESSES.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: Limits of results for oversight methods like debate obtained on multiple choice questions about short science fiction stories that the judges have not read

open_obligations: Check that the 'reading comprehension task' argument is aimed at Khan et al. and not only Michael et al. (2023)
Confirm Khan et al.'s limitation section concedes the information-only expertise gap
in.other_title: Kenton et al. argue Khan et al.'s quote-only information asymmetry limits what debate tests show
in.rationale: Khan et al. themselves note their expertise gap is only information access; the authors argue this setup is artificial and limits conclusions about debate. The passage is an argument about the cited setup, not new data on it, and it makes the same point as Khan et al.'s stated limitation: the gap between the judge and debaters should ideally arise from differences in various capabilities, not only information asymmetry. So SUPPORTS.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether an information-only expertise gap on QuALITY is an adequate test of debate as scalable oversight

open_obligations: Check that the statement 'All of those works' is meant to include Khan et al. and not only Radhakrishnan (2023) and Michael et al. (2023)
Confirm Khan et al.'s own limitation section states the information-only expertise gap that this link concerns
in.other_title: Kirchner et al. call Khan et al.'s QuALITY debate setting artificial: privileged information, not capability gap
in.rationale: Khan et al. acknowledge that their expertise gap is only information access; the authors characterize this setting as more artificial than their capability-gap math setting and describe the difference in it as privileged information rather than a capability gap. This agrees with Khan et al.'s stated limitation rather than arguing that it is flawed, so SUPPORTS, limited to the information-access part of that limitation.
in.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: Whether information-asymmetric QuALITY debate is a good proxy for oversight across a capability gap; covers only the target's statement that its expertise gap is access to information, not its point about RLHF-tuned models

text: The authors state that in their setup the difference between strong and weak models is only access to information, whereas future stronger models may differ in reasoning ability or other skills. They also state they evaluate RLHF-fine-tuned models with a propensity for honesty, so it is unclear whether debate will be suitable for deceptive models.
title: Expertise gap is only information access; RLHF debaters have an honesty propensity
